sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Poliahu** ​(*poliahu*) — ‌Snow, ‌Mauna Kea ​· ​Cloaked bosom ​— ​belongs to ​the Polynesian ‌tradition, ​where it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the ‌domain "Snow, ​Mauna ‌Kea". The ​name ​means "Cloaked ​bosom"[^1].

​**Poliahu** is ​the ‌Hawaiian goddess ​of **snow ‌— ​the beautiful ‌and ​powerful mistress ‌of ​Mauna Kea's ‌summit**, ​whose white ​mantle ‌crowns the ‌highest ‌mountain in ​the ​Pacific and ‌whose duel ​with ​the volcano ‌goddess ​Pele for ​possession ‌of the ​mountain ‌is one ​of ​Hawai'i's most ​beloved ​and most ‌retold legends.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​records the ‌canonical ​scholarly spelling ​**Poliahu** ‌and serves ‌its ‌temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/poliahu/). The ‌displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*poliahu* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters: no ​recovered ‌diacritics or ​special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. The ​work ​here is ​consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​modern Polynesian ​orthographies; ​macron ​usage follows ​each ‌tradition’s reference ​dictionaries. ​Etymologically ‌the name ​means ‌"Cloaked ​bosom"[^1].

The ‌canonical ​spelling **Poliahu** ​matches ​the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*poliahu* contains ‌the ​same ‌letters, so ​no ‌lost ​diacritics or ​encoding ‌transition is ‌claimed. ‌The ​editorial work ​is ‌to ​fix one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization ‌and provenance, ​and ‌keep ​the original ​evidence ​visible. The ​displayed ‌form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ​description computed ​from ‌the displayed ‌form ‌itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**p** → ​**P** ​— Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**o** ​→ **o** ​— ‌Same
- ​**l** → ​**l** ​— Same
- ‌**i** ​→ ‌**i** — ​Same
- ‌**a** ​→ **a** ‌— ‌Same
- **h** ​→ ​**h** ​— Same
- ​**u** ‌→ ‌**u** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/poliahu/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**poliahu** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Poliahu.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Poliahu" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Poliahu" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"poliahu" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Poliahu ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Poliahu ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Poliahu ‌place ​snow, mauna ​kea ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Poliahu ‌appears ​in polynesian ‌tradition ​as ​snow, mauna ​kea. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Cloaked ​bosom", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Poliahu ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Poliahu ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Poliahu ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Poliahu ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Poliahu, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​snow ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Poliahu ​embodies a ‌wonder unique ‌in ​the Pacific: ​**snow in ​the ​tropics**. Hawaiians, ​meeting white ‌on ​a tropical ​summit, made ‌it ​a goddess ‌— and ​the ‌making says ​something precise ​about ​Polynesian theology, ​which found ​the ‌sacred in ​the anomalous ‌and ​the extreme. ‌Where Pele ​is ‌appetite and ​eruption, Poliahu ‌is ​reserve and ​stillness; the ‌two ‌goddesses are ‌the island's ​two ​temperatures, and ‌the myth ​grants ​each her ‌jurisdiction. There ​is ​also a ‌geography lesson ​folded into ‌the ​myth: the ​legend's battle-scarred ​terrain ​matches real ‌volcanic features ‌reaching ​toward the ‌snows, so ​the ​story functions ‌as memory ‌of ‌eruptions older ‌than any ​chant. ‌But beyond ​scholarship, Poliahu ​endures ​because she ‌is beautiful ​in ​the strict ​sense — ‌a ​presence that ​caps the ​island ‌with white, ​that can ‌bless ​a sled ‌race or ​bury ‌a valley ‌in hail. ​She ​is what ​a mountain ​means ‌when the ‌mountain is ​loved.[^1]
